name: ping
description: Sends ICMP echo requests to a host and measures round-trip time and packet loss — the first tool for "is it reachable?".

flags.description: Stop after N packets (otherwise ping runs forever — Ctrl+C to stop).
Interval between packets (default 1s; sub-second needs root).
Send via a specific interface or source IP.
Packet size in bytes (default 56 + 28 header = 84 on the wire).

examples.output:
PING google.com (142.250.74.142) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from ...: icmp_seq=1 ttl=118 time=8.42 ms
--- google.com ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss
examples.explanation: Four probes with summary: 0% loss, ~8 ms round trip. This proves DNS, routing, AND the remote host all work.
Pings the local gateway by IP — if this fails but the cable/link is fine, the problem is local.
If this works but domain names fail, the problem is DNS, not connectivity.

about: The ping diagnostic ladder: 1) ping 127.0.0.1 (your TCP/IP stack), 2) ping your gateway (local network), 3) ping a public IP like 8.8.8.8 (internet routing), 4) ping a domain (DNS). Where it first fails tells you where the problem is. Many servers block ICMP for security, so a failed ping does not always mean the host is down.
useCases: Isolating local vs DNS vs routing problems.
mistakes: Concluding "server down" from a failed ping when ICMP is merely firewalled — test the actual service port instead.
Letting an unbounded ping run in scripts; always use -c.
warnings: Continuous ping without -c generates endless traffic; in scripts always bound it.
